claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start the assessment by getting the first question for you.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! To start the assessment, I need to understand the age of your child or children. 

**How old is the child you're claiming Child Benefit for?** 

Please let me know:
- The child's name (or names if you have more than one child)
- Their age (or date of birth)

The eligibility depends on the child's age:
- **Under 16 years old**: Usually automatic qualification
- **16-19 years old**: They need to be in full-time education or approved training
- **20 years old or over**: Generally not eligible

Please provide these details so I can continue with the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm looking to claim Child Benefit for my son Alex. He's 17 years old and lives at home with me.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thanks for that information! So you're looking to claim Child Benefit for **Alex, who is 17 years old**. That's helpful context.

Since Alex is 17, he falls into the **16-19 age category**. For young people in this age group, I need to check whether Alex is in full-time education or approved training, as this affects eligibility.

**Is Alex currently:**
1. In full-time education (such as school, college, or university)?
2. In an approved training scheme or apprenticeship?
3. Not in education or training?

Please let me know Alex's current status so I can continue the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Alex recently started an apprenticeship actually - he's doing a trade apprenticeship.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! That's great news for your claim. Since Alex is 17 and doing an approved apprenticeship, he qualifies as being in approved training, which means he meets the requirements for the 16-19 age group.

Let me navigate through the assessment to confirm his eligibility.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! Now I need to confirm that Alex is currently in education or training. Based on what you've told me, Alex is doing an apprenticeship, so let me proceed.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Now I need to check some details about Alex's apprenticeship to make sure it meets the eligibility requirements. For 16-19 year olds in training, Child Benefit is only paid if the training is "approved" (non-advanced) education or training.

**A few questions about Alex's apprenticeship:**

1. **What level is the apprenticeship?** For example:
   - A standard apprenticeship (typically NVQ Level 2-3)?
   - A higher apprenticeship (Level 4+)?
   - A different type?

2. **Is it full-time training?** (At least 12 hours per week of supervised study/training with the employer)

3. **Is the apprenticeship being funded by the employer?** Or is it part of a government-supported scheme?

These details will help me confirm whether it qualifies as approved training for Child Benefit purposes.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: It's a standard trade apprenticeship - he's training to be a carpenter. It's full-time, so definitely more than 12 hours a week. As for funding, I think it's through one of those government apprenticeship schemes, but his employer is involved too. Is that a problem?

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
That sounds like a standard apprenticeship setup! Let me clarify the funding aspect, as it's important for eligibility.

**A quick question about the funding:**

When you say it's through a government apprenticeship scheme with employer involvement, can you confirm:

1. **Is Alex being paid a wage/salary by the employer** as part of the apprenticeship (even if it's the apprentice minimum wage)?
2. **Or is the employer funding the training costs** but Alex isn't receiving payment directly from them?

This distinction matters because:
- If Alex is an **employee being paid by the employer** (even apprentice wages) while doing the training, that's typically fine for Child Benefit purposes
- If it's **purely employer-funded training with no wages**, that could affect eligibility

What's the arrangement with Alex's payment/wages?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Oh yes, he's definitely getting paid by the employer - he gets the apprentice wage. He's working for them as an employee while doing his training.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! That clarifies things. Since Alex is being paid as an employee (receiving the apprentice wage) while undertaking full-time training through a government-backed scheme, this is standard approved training for Child Benefit purposes.

Let me continue through the assessment:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good! Now I need to check how many hours per week Alex is working in the apprenticeship.

**How many hours per week is Alex working as part of his apprenticeship?**

This is important because the rule is that 16+ year olds in approved training (like Alex) are eligible as long as they're not working 24+ hours per week. Since he's in approved training, this shouldn't be a problem, but I need to confirm the hours.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's working full-time as part of the apprenticeship - it's a proper full-time job with the training included.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thanks for confirming. Since Alex is in a full-time apprenticeship as a proper employee, he's definitely working more than 24 hours per week. However, because he's in **approved training** (the standard trade apprenticeship we confirmed earlier), the 24-hour rule doesn't apply to him in the same way.

Let me navigate forward based on his approved training status:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check another eligibility criteria:

**Is Alex currently receiving any of the following benefits in his own right:**
- Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)?
- Universal Credit (as a self-employed or employed person)?

Or is he **not receiving** these types of benefits?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not receiving any benefits like that - nothing in his own name.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Let me continue:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I need to ask an important question about the apprenticeship rules:

**Which country is Alex doing his apprenticeship in - England, Scotland, or Wales?**

This matters because there are specific regional rules:
- **England**: Unfortunately, all types of apprenticeships (standard, intermediate, advanced, higher, degree) are currently not eligible for Child Benefit
- **Scotland**: Modern Apprenticeships are not eligible
- **Wales**: Foundation Apprenticeships ARE eligible, but most other apprenticeships are not

Where is Alex's apprenticeship based?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's doing it in England - we live here in England.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I appreciate you clarifying that. I need to let you know about an important eligibility rule for England.

Unfortunately, in **England**, the rules state that **all types of apprenticeships** (including standard trade apprenticeships like Alex's carpentry apprenticeship) currently **disqualify a child from receiving Child Benefit**.

This is a specific regional rule that applies regardless of the quality of the training or how well Alex is progressing.

Let me navigate to confirm this outcome:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Based on the official Child Benefit eligibility rules, I'm sorry to inform you that:

**Alex is not eligible for Child Benefit** because he has started an apprenticeship in England.

**Why this applies:**
- While Alex meets many of the eligibility criteria (he's 17, in full-time training, receiving an apprentice wage, and not receiving other disqualifying benefits), the specific rule in England is that **all apprenticeships result in ineligibility for Child Benefit**
- This is a direct disqualification that takes precedence over the general eligibility for 16-19 year olds in training

**Important information:**
- If Alex **stops** the apprenticeship and returns to full-time education (such as college or sixth form) that isn't an apprenticeship, he would become eligible again
- If you were previously receiving Child Benefit for Alex **before** he started the apprenticeship, you would need to notify HMRC about the change in circumstances, and payments would stop

**Next steps:**
- You can contact HMRC Child Benefit office to inform them of this change if applicable
- You may want to review whether there are any other children you'd like to claim for
- For more information, visit: https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit/eligibility

Is there anything else I can help you with, or do you have any other children you'd like me to assess?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Oh, I see. That's disappointing, but thank you for explaining it clearly. No, Alex is my only child, so I guess that's it then. I appreciate you taking the time to go through everything with me.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
You're very welcome! I'm glad I could walk you through the assessment clearly, even though the outcome wasn't what you were hoping for. It's understandable that it's disappointing, but I appreciate you taking the time to get clarity on where you stand.

Let me record the final outcome for your records:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
If your circumstances change in the future—for example, if Alex were to move to a different form of full-time education—please feel free to come back and we can reassess. 

Best of luck to Alex with his carpentry apprenticeship! It's great that he's pursuing a skilled trade. If you have any other questions in the future, don't hesitate to reach out.
